utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please continue with your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court. Before I continue where I left off, on the last day we were here I had indicated in response to an objection by learned counsel Mr. O'Sullivan that I would check what the situation was in respect to Mr. Tanic's statement and what parts are admissible. And I am to report that on this occasion Mr. O'Sullivan is correct. The situation in respect of Mr. Tanic's statement is that only paragraphs 1 to 45 would be admissible; the remainder were to provide context in respect to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When we broke last, Your Honours, I was referring the Court to some of the evidence relating to the knowledge, both that could be inferred and directly, that the accused Sainovic would have and did have about the offences that were being committed in Kosovo and the likelihood that these offences would continue to be committed. And we were -- I was referring to the meeting on the 17th of May, 1999, and it is submitted that his knowledge is further evidenced by his attendance at that meeting where it was reported that crimes had been committed by members of the VJ and by volunteers, and Serb officials also stated that a group of volunteers that entered Grocka without the usual training or check-ups. Mr. Vasiljevic who gave testimony about this meeting notes or noted from the meeting that there was a reference to the SAJ integrating into other -- integrating into the organisation itself groups and forces which had not fulfilled the requirements of serving within the MUP. And this is from his written statement P2592 and 8873. From this it may be inferred that Mr. Sainovic was aware of the nature of the reserve forces and their propensity to commit crimes, and in addition to this army officials at the meeting reported that the forces responsible for the crimes at Podujevo had moved into Gnjilane without any investigation or punishment, and once in Gnjilane these forces committed additional crimes. The officials at the meetings were also told by army reporting personnel that the meeting that Radosavljevic's unit, which included Arkan's Tigers, had committed crimes in the Kosovo area. So this is one occasion on which Mr. Sainovic received substantial information about ongoing crimes committed by forces of the FRY and Serbia, in particular volunteer forces or forces incorporated into the MUP units and their propensity as well to commit crimes. In addition to this, there is evidence again in P2594 from Mr. Vasiljevic, a statement of Mr. Vasiljevic, that there was at the disposal of Mr. Sainovic a reporting system where all senior members of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo and the civilian structures in Kosovo reported to Mr. Sainovic on events in Kosovo during regular meetings, and they transformed his instructions into combat operations and activities, and these led to the crimes which are charged in the indictment. Indeed, Mr. Loncar -- sorry, General Loncar testified that Mr. Sainovic insisted on being informed in a timely manner of incidents in the field, especially those involving many victims. When big incidents occurred such as the events in Racak in January 1999, Mr. Pavkovic and General Lukic were required to contact General [sic] Sainovic directly, and this is the testimony of Dusan Loncar at transcript page numbers 7576 to 7577. In that part of the testimony, Mr. -- General Loncar also indicated that even when some of the senior officers on the ground were or sought to report incidents to Mr. Sainovic about the -- or sought to report to Mr. Sainovic about the events at Racak, he clearly was aware of the details of the events before many of these persons, and this indicates that a system of reporting or this system of reporting that he had at his disposal was sufficiently efficient to inform him of what was happening on the ground and he would be aware of the events referred to in the indictment. In the opening citation from Mr. -- from General Vasiljevic's statement I referred to General Vasiljevic's assessment that Mr. Sainovic was report -- receiving reports from persons as high as General Lazarevic, General Lukic on a very regular basis, probably a daily basis because of the nature and topics, 24-hour reporting that occurred in the course of that meeting. And I have also referred the Court to the many meetings he attended with senior personnel in which he would have been informed. In addition, his other interactions with international interlocutors supply additional grounds for inferring that Mr. Sainovic was aware of the criminal activity in Kosovo. As the evidence or as recalled by General DZ, for example, the meeting of the 4th of December, 1992, Mr. Sainovic was informed that the police in Malisevo were harassing Albanians and were therefore part of the problem. Mr. Sainovic not only refused to diminish the police presence but also failed to investigate the allegations made by General DZ and this is in the course of his testimony at pages 7777 to 7782. Mr. Sainovic, according to General Naumann, was also present at a meeting during which Mr. Milosevic was given a list of violations of the October agreement which were committed by Serb forces. This is in General Naumann's statement at P2512 and also his testimony -- I beg your pardon, P2512 is his testimony in the Milosevic case and it's at 7008 to 7009. The -- a similar observation has been made in respect to his meeting with the Kosovar Albanian leaders as has been made in respect to this very same meeting and Mr. Milutinovic's state of mind or awareness as a result of that meeting. Again, without going into the submission again, these were the leaders, acknowledged leaders, of the Kosovar Albanian people. And both Mr. Merovci and Mr. Rugova, according to the evidence, stated that Mr. Sainovic was present when Mr. Rugova made complaints to Mr. Milutinovic about members of the forces of the FRY, the MUP in particular, forcing Albanians from their homes and destroying their homes. And that is the statement of Mr. Merovci, P2588, at paragraph 72; and the statement of Mr. Rugova, P2613, at page 11. So the -- this ongoing knowledge of -- in circumstances where he did not act to end or prevent the continuing offences in Kosovo, indicates, it is respectfully submitted and it is an inference which the open to the Court and therefore legitimately before the Court, that Mr. Sainovic shared the intent of the joint criminal enterprise, that he shared the intent to carry out the goals of the JCE to recast the ethnic make-up of Kosovo. According to Ratomir Tanic at 6325 to 6 of the transcript, as early as the spring of 1998 Mr. Sainovic was no longer interested or committed to the peaceful resolution of the problems in Kosovo. In addition, Klaus Naumann testified that at a meeting with internationals around the 24th of October, 1998, either Mr. Sainovic, or if not him, Mr. Milosevic in the presence of Mr. Sainovic made statements regarding the birth-rates of Kosovar Albanians and the need to strike a better ethnic balance. This is at paragraph 29 of the statement of Mr. Naumann, which is P1767. Whether Mr. Sainovic made the statement or it was made by Mr. Milosevic in his presence, it indicates his at least tacit agreement to the stated position. I have already referred the Court to some of the evidence about the de facto exercise of authority and power by Mr. Sainovic, and I will wrap up by referring to some other items of evidence which demonstrates, as submitted before, that he exercised command authority, effective authority, as Mr. Milosevic's representative in Kosovo. He was, in his official capacity, Mr. Milosevic's representative. He had been sent from early 1998 to Kosovo by Mr. Milosevic on at least two fact-finding missions and had the authority to report back to Mr. Milosevic about the situation or his insight into the situation on the ground in Kosovo. This can be gleaned from his interview, P605 at page 27, 28. In addition to the example I gave earlier, Veton Surroi observed, in respect to the Rambouillet negotiations, that whenever direct consultations with Mr. Milosevic was required, Mr. Sainovic would be the one to fly to Belgrade to speak with him. And in addition to this, in addition to the power to approve and to lay the guide-lines within which the generals on the ground could prepare the plans or the -- the strategy of the campaign on the ground, there were occasions in which Mr. Sainovic directly interfered or directly exercised authority over the VJ. We have seen already that he did, to a significant degree, directly exercise authority over the MUP at his presence at MUP meetings, giving specific instructions, and that is from the evidence, as I discussed earlier, of Mr. Cvetic. And there are specific instances where he, as head of the Joint Command, exercised this sort of authority over the VJ. General Naumann testified that prior to Mr. Milosevic's extremely reluctant and late signature on the 28th of October, 1998, record of meeting between NATO representatives and the FRY and Serbia, Mr. Sainovic signed, was a lone signatory who could sign on behalf of both the VJ and the FRY. Ratomir Tanic at 6373 to 6374 of the transcript testified that Mr. Pavkovic -- sorry, it's General Pavkovic took orders from Mr. Sainovic to engage military units to assist the MUP and to give the MUP mortars and tanks, contrary to constitutional provisions. And we see that General Vasiljevic, in his testimony in the Milosevic case, that is P2589, at 16429 to 16430 of that transcript, said that Mr. Sainovic would also engage in the issuance of precise orders and this, he said, was evidenced by his ordering of detachments on Mount Rudnik to attack Laus in 1998, and Your Honours have also heard about the complaint by the former Chief of Staff of the VJ, General Perisic, about Sainovic's directing VJ forces which is a letter, P717. In addition to his exercise of de facto command responsibilities over the VJ and the FRY, there's evidence of General Loncar, that Mr. Sainovic, together with Mr. Andjelkovic, worked together to establish a local police force in Kosovo and also, as head of the Joint Command, Mr. Sainovic exercised authority over the local defence. The items of evidence I've outlined, Your Honours, I respectfully submit goes to -- submit -- goes to establish that Mr. Sainovic shared the intent of the joint criminal enterprise, was aware of the persecutory conduct of the forces of the FRY and Serbia against Kosovar Albanians prior to the 23rd of March, 1999, and after the 23rd of March, 1999; and he exercised his authority with all this knowledge to further the joint criminal enterprise; that he participated in the planning of the activities resulting in the expulsion of the Kosovar Albanians; he aided and abetted the parties involved in these expulsions. His continued failure to take appropriate steps, which I'll come to shortly, encouraged and instigated continued perpetration of these offences. I'd like, with your leave, now move to the evidence in respect to Mr. Lukic, and I would do it, I think, conveniently if I make some general submissions first and then move to the specific complaints or submissions raised by learned counsel for the Defence. The Prosecution's case is that General Lukic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise charged in the indictment and that he actively contributed to its implementation. As chief of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, he was the highest-ranking police officer of the MUP in Kosovo during the indictment period. He participated in the joint criminal enterprise by using the MUP staff to plan, direct, and coordinate the activities and operations of the MUP in Kosovo. He issued orders and instructions to subordinates in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise, pursuant to instructions from senior members of the joint criminal enterprise including the Joint Command. Mr. Lukic held key -- held a key position in the MUP chain of command. He was appointed as head of the MUP staff in Kosovo on 11th of May, 1998, by decision signed by the head of the MUP public security sector, General Djordjevic. That's P1252. And he remained in that position throughout the war in 1999, and that can be determined from P1811. As head of the MUP staff, he commanded, controlled, and exercised authority over the MUP and its subordinate units in Kosovo. P1251, the decision on the formation of the MUP staff dated the 15th of May, 1998, and signed by General Djordjevic, states the mandate of the MUP staff, and that was a plan to organise, guide, and coordinate the work of the ministry's organisational units and the work units posted or attached to it during their engagement in the suppression of terrorism in the territory of the Kosovo province. And it is significant that it's -- the authority extended not only to the units domicile, as it were, the units posted in Kosovo and Metohija on a long-term basis, but also units that were seconded to it or sent to it from other areas or other jurisdictions of the MUP. The MUP staff was expanded in June of 1990, bringing the RDB and the RJB together in the MUP staff headquarters in Pristina. The expanded staff also included the chiefs of Kosovo's seven secretariats of internal affairs. P1505 is a decision to establish a ministerial staff, and it indicates, as I just submitted, the various groups that were subordinated to the MUP staff in Kosovo. Ljubinko Cvetic, the former chief of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP stated in evidence that in practice whatever special units such as special police units, the PJP, special anti-terrorist units, SAJ, operational sweep groups, or the special operational units, that's the OPGs or JSOs, were employed or engaged in operations in Kosovo, these units fell under the command and structure of the MUP staff. The MUP staff would issue orders to the commanders of these units, and that is at pages 8073 to 5 of the transcript. The MUP staff from their control, direction, and ordering of these various elements that we are told by the crime base witnesses committed the various crimes against them in Kosovo. The MUP staff played a crucial [Realtime transcript read in error "Velika Krusa"] role in implementing the joint criminal enterprise in their control of the activities of these groups. And through the MUP staff Mr. Lukic planned, directed, and coordinated these groups and their activities in Kosovo. He received his from his superiors, who were also members of the JCE, and he implemented the JCE by communicating and directing the SUPs and the MUP units, the special MUP units that were deployed, in Kosovo, that's by communicating to and directing these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet, but I think that would be correct. In his interview with the OTP Mr. -- General Lukic stated that the role of the Joint Command was to coordinate police and army duties in Kosovo and that it was headed by Mr. Sainovic. And his interview is P948 and the part I'm referring to is pages 34 to 35. He said that the members of the Joint Command which included the head of the MUP staff, that's himself; the commander of the 3rd Army; and other persons would hold joint meetings to review the security situation and exchange information. According to Mr. Cvetic at 8080 and 8194 to 95 of the transcript, as a member of the Joint Command, General Lukic was in charge of implementing the decisions adopted by the joint staff, by the MUP staff. General Lukic regularly attended Joint Command meetings and briefings on MUP-related matters taking part in discussions on the operations to be conducted. This is what Mr. -- General Lukic himself said in his interview at pages 35 to 36. He and other members of the Joint Command planned, ordered, and coordinated joint operations to be conducted by military and police units in Kosovo. For example, without going into these documents too much because they were cited previously, Exhibit 1968 is a Joint Command order of the 24th of March, 1999, instructing the Pristina Corps to support MUP forces in anti-terrorist operations conducted in the Drenica sector. Another example is Exhibit P1998 [sic] which is a Joint Command operation report of November 1998 which evidences the role of the Joint Command in coordinating the activities of both the MUP and the VJ. General Lukic, it is submitted, participated in the planning and coordination of joint MUP/VJ anti-terrorist operations in 1998 and 1999, which involved the use of excessive force against the Kosovo Albanians and ultimately the use of force designed to expel them or expel a substantial part of them from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The evidence from the crime base witnesses shows that the anti-terrorist operations as they are naturally described in the police documents consistently involved the use of excessive force against the Kosovar Albanian population. During his tour of Kosovo in 1999, John Crosland, a British Defence Attache, observed joint MUP/VJ clearing operations against Albanian villages, and this is his statement, P2645, paragraphs 37 to 42. He said that he, himself, saw between 200 and 300 villages burnt throughout 1998 and into 1999. Crops were just wantonly burned; businesses of all sorts, for example petrol stations and shops, were looted. And within the towns of Decani, Pec, Djakovica, the Albanian areas were completely burned up. And he described the standard tactics employed in these operations, and it was that there were MUP special units, such as PJPs and SAJ units, entering villages and settlements on foot while the VJ would establish a cordon and provide fire support with tank and artillery. We respectfully submit that the trial record is replete with evidence that the MUP and VJ units employed similar tactics in 1999 which resulted in the commission of the crimes. In early 1999, Richard Ciaglinski observed a similar practice in a joint VJ/MUP operation. He stated that the normal method of operation was that the MUP would lead operation and provide infantry soldiers on the ground, while the VJ's role was to provide heavy fire support. And this is at page 12 of his statement, which is P2488. And Mr. Hannis also enumerated the crime base witnesses who also spoke about joint MUP/VJ attacks on their villages during the course of which the local population was forcibly expelled. The evidence, as I've indicated, is that General Lukic was one of the directors, one of the senior participants, senior planners and coordinators, of these assaults. General Lukic also assisted in the arming of the non-Albanian civilians in Kosovo. We have seen some of the reports including those that I discussed earlier that were tendered through Mr. Cvetic discussing the participation of what were described as the armed Siptar -- armed non-Siptar population in police operations, police and VJ operations. The evidence demonstrates that the MUP used local citizens and those with MUP reservist status in village defence units, Exhibit P1064, which is a July 1998 Joint Command instruction on defending populated areas, gave MUP command over local defence units. By July 1998, the situation was such that General Lukic could send a letter to all the secretariats of the interior, the SUPs, attaching extracts from a register of weapons issued by the VJ to: "Citizens engage in defence of villages and cities through the reserve police squads in the municipalities" and these fell under the seven SUPs. In that letter he directed the SUP chiefs to update their reserve police unit records to support their defence plans. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I understand that submission, Mr. Stamp. It may again be a misrepresentation in the transcript. "By July 1998 the situation was such that General Lukic could send a letter to the SUPs attaching extracts from a register of weapons issued by the VJ" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, I'll put it in this way. P1115 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1150"] is a letter sent by General Lukic to the heads of all the SUPs. In which he attached extracts from a register of weapons that were issued by the VJ to various citizens, and he in that letter directed the SUP chiefs to update their reserve police unit records in respect to citizens who had received these weapons. The submission is that this letter, P1115, indicate that General Lukic through his position as head of the MUP staff in Kosovo, also exercised control over these so-called armed non-Siptar members of the population that had been issued weapons. Indeed, an accompanying page of that exhibit, covering only the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP area, notes that 7.436 weapons were assigned -- I'm sorry, an accompanying page indicates that 7.436 weapons were assigned to the six municipalities which the MUP covered. So this shows that the military, the VJ, provided weapons to these units and these units were formed around the reserve MUP units and that they were under the control of the MUP staff. This is also supported by the evidence of Mr. Cvetic at pages 8054 to 8546 of the transcript. The -- two of the exhibits that refer to the use of these armed civilians in police operations are 1968 and P1878. And Mr. Cvetic explained the expression "armed non-Siptar population" in these orders and also said at 8090 of the transcript that in past Serbian population in the Drenica area was armed and assigned to either VJ or MUP units. In addition to this evidence shows that -- it is submitted that contrary, to law volunteers who came to Kosovo were armed and were engaged by the MUP. Exhibit 1990, the minutes of the MUP staff meeting of the 17th of February, 1999, records instructions of the MUP minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic as to how to approach and engage volunteers that appeared in Kosovo indicating that such men were to be retained and included in the MUP as reserve police. You'll remember the evidence of Mr. Cvetic, who said that contrary to what happened, the law was that the MUP or the law did not allow the MUP to engage volunteers; only the VJ was allowed to engage volunteers. And Cvetic recalled that at a MUP meeting or at a meeting of the MUP staff on the 17th of March, 1999, General Lukic said that in case volunteers appeared in Kosovo, such men were to be retained and incorporated into MUP operations once the war began. And that's at 8099 of the transcript. The -- this reference is also relevant, Your Honours, to the issue of failure to prevent. As happens in circumstances like these, a lot of the evidence in respect to different elements or different areas of the case merge or overlap, and I mention this so that I won't have to go over that document again, evidence, Your Honours, is also that General Lukic in the planning, instigating, and ordering the concealment by members of the MUP and subordinate MUP -- subordinate units of the crime of murder. The evidence shows that General Lukic was involved in coordinating the transfer of bodies of Kosovar Albanians in mass grave sites to Serbia. Bozidar Protic, one of the drivers involved in the transfer of the bodies, testified that Mr. Lukic contacted him on at least three occasions and gave him instructions as to where to pick up and transport the bodies and that he acted on these instructions. Credibility issues were raised in respect to Mr. Protic, in particular why it is the first time he spoke or was interviewed in 2001 or 2000 he did not mention Mr. Lukic; he explained that. Here it is submitted it is not -- or now it is submitted it is not the appropriate time for us to weigh these fine issues of credibility, but I would -- I would submit this, that his testimony about his contact with General Lukic before he was engaged to remove the bodies, during the period when he was engaged to remove the body when he spoke to General Lukic on a few occasions, and after that period when both General Lukic and General Djordjevic, he spoke to both of them in respect to certain arrangements, is evidence at this stage on which a Court can act to show that General Lukic participated in the concealment of these bodies. And I remind the Court that the evidence is that the first shipment occurred somewhere in the first week, first few days of April; that is very shortly after the hostilities commenced. Not much has been said in these submissions about the bodies, so if I may, I will not discuss them at this stage in detail except to point out that well over 800 bodies of Kosovar Albanians were found at several graves in Kosovo. 828 bodies; I've found the figure. Batajnica had 705 bodies. Some of them, 300 of them, were identified as victims from Meja and Suva Reka, charged in the indictment. From the evidence it is clear that these bodies were transported there within just a few days after the alleged offences. Petrovo Selo had 75 bodies, 22 of which were identified as victims of the Izbica massacre, and at Lake Perucac there were 48 bodies, all of them victims from Kosovo. Your Honours, 828 bodies recovered in these mass graves in Serbia that were identified are persons whose names appear on the ICRC list of missing persons in Kosovo during the indictment period. This ICRC list was incorporated in the list of the UNMIK organisation for missing persons and was tendered through Dr. Baraybar. I thought I had noted the number, the exhibit number, but this number is wrong and I will submit the number shortly. And most of these persons from the scientific examination of the remains, particularly in some cases bone fragments, were killed by gun-shot wounds. Much can reasonably be inferred, it is respectfully submitted, from the foregoing in respect to Mr. Lukic's intent and that he shared the intent of the joint criminal enterprise and shared the intent to cover up crimes. That he knew that the crimes committed in Kosovo by the forces of the FRY and Serbia during the indictment period, he knew of them and he was aware that he, his actions were contributing to the commission of the crimes. He was informed of the massive displacement of Kosovo Albanians and the perpetration of numerous other crimes through the reporting systems of the MUP at his attendance at the various staff meetings. Indeed it is respectfully submitted that it is inconceivable that the police officer in charge of operations on the ground in an area the size of Kosovo would not be aware of such large-scale crimes and such large-scale movements of people. The evidence in the trial record shows that at all times relevant to the indictment, the MUP had effective and functioning reporting structures in Kosovo. General Lukic issued instructions, detailed instructions, to his immediate subordinates to ensure that the periodic reports, including daily reports, were sent up the chain of command and that he was kept fully apprised of the developments on the ground and of the progress of operations. Exhibit 2528 is such an order. Ljubinko Cvetic stated that all police stations and OUPs had to brief the SUPs and that based on General Lukic's instructions, the secretariats compiled information and forwarded it up the chain of command. In February 1999, the police stations throughout Kosovo ordered to report significant incidents directly and immediately to the MUP operation centre, in the MUP headquarters in Belgrade and to the MUP staff for Kosovo. And this reinforced Lukic's control of the situation. This is P1092. Exhibits P1990 are minutes of MUP meetings or is the minutes of MUP meetings or a meeting dated the 17th of February, and it shows that reports were made. And again Exhibit P1998, further minutes of the MUP meeting on the 4th of April, 1999, has Lukic reminding the SUP chief and unit commanders of their duty to report. Lukic would also have been kept aware of the situation by his interactions with senior members of the JCE at MUP staff meetings. Many of these meetings were attended by Mr. Sainovic, the head of the Joint Command; the minister of internal affairs, Mr. Stojiljkovic; the head of the RDB, Mr. Djordjevic; the head of police operations or administration in the RJB, Mr. Stevanovic; and the command of the MUP special units. These meetings and what Mr. Lukic reported and had to say at these meetings indicate that he had a hands-on involvement and control of affairs that were occurring on the ground. General Lukic also knew of the likelihood that MUP units would commit crimes in 1998 due to the widespread reporting from many sources of allegations of crimes committed in Kosovo in 1998. He was informed of crimes committed by forces under his command in 1998 through numerous complaints voiced by international observers - this applies to all of the accused. The allegations were publicly and prominently raised in United Nations by human rights organisations. Fred Abrahams testified about making several reports, or forwarding several reports to the police authorities, domestic and foreign media, foreign diplomats. The entire world, as is alleged in the indictment, was aware that there were at least allegations of serious violations of humanitarian rights of Kosovar Albanians. Indeed, this was the stated, the ostensible reason for the threat of NATO involvement in Kosovo. On one specific occasion, during a meeting between General Lukic and General DZ in December 1998, General DZ informed General Lukic that the KVM had received unconfirmed reports of the use of excessive force by the police in village searches in Kosovo Polje. Lukic sought to refute these allegations. Shaun Byrnes, the former head of the United States KDOM stated that in the summer of 1998 he met with General Lukic on a regular basis and informed him and his team that KDOM, US-KDOM, had observed MUP forces forcibly expelling Kosovar Albanians from their villages, destroying property, and torching houses. On one occasion himself, Byrnes, personally observed this. Lukic's reaction to Byrnes' complaints was either to dismiss them as untrue or to say that the MUP actions were carried out in response to KLA attacks. This is the transcript of the evidence of Shaun Byrnes from 12148 to 12153. Apart from engaging in what Mr. Cvetic said was an unlawful practice of receiving volunteers into the MUP, General Lukic also knew of and approved of incorporation into the MUP of volunteer groups that had a history of allegations of involvements in serious crimes against civilians in other conflicts and also in the Kosovo conflict in 1998. General Lukic approved the integration of about 128 members of the Skorpions into the SAJ as reservists in March 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Goran Stoparic, a former member of the Skorpions, stated that his unit, upon their arrival in Kosovo, was issued with MUP uniforms, equipment, and attached to the SAJ. Soon after their deployment in Kosovo, members of the Skorpions executed a group of women and children in Podujevo and they were subsequently sent back to Serbia. However, in April 1999, 108 members of the same unit were redeployed in Kosovo under the SAJ command and they operated in Kosovo until May 1999. When one reviews the reporting system that Mr. -- that General Lukic had at his disposal and the level of detail that he could furnish when he himself did is reporting up, it is a clear inference, it is submitted, that he must have known of the deployment and redeployment of this unit under his command. In addition, Exhibit 1505, which is a decision to establish the Ministerial Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism dated June 1999 shows that one of the members of the MUP staff in 1998 was Milorad Ulemek, also known as Legija. Legija was the operations or the head of special operations of the MUP staff.

The date of the exhibit is actually June 1998, 16th of June, 1998, and it refers to this person at that time as being the assistant head of special operations of the MUP staff. utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate having to do this again, but the statement of Vasiljevic does not refer to Legija's unit, it refers to a unit called Legija, which I think is a significant point and I'll have more points at the conclusion of Mr. Stamp's submissions regarding other misstatements of the evidence that have been made thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As the head of the MUP staff, General Lukic had the material ability to prevent crimes from being committed as well as enforce discipline among MUP units, including special units. A functioning discipline and justice system existed to ensure discipline and respect for the law in the MUP; however, despite his knowledge of the widespread and systematic crimes committed by the forces under his command in 1998 and 1999, he failed to take substantive measures from prevent his subordinates from committing further crimes or to punish them for the crimes they had committed over the protracted period of time in Kosovo. In addition to the inference that in doing so he furthered the joint criminal enterprise, it is also submitted that from this the only reasonable inference to be drawn is that he intended these crimes to occur. And it is therefore submitted in light of the evidence of the offences committed by the MUP on the ground in Kosovo that a reasonable Trial Chamber could find that General Lukic is responsible as a co-perpetrator for the commission of the crimes charged in the indictment. General Lukic, it is submitted, is also responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) for ordering, instigating, aiding and abetting the crimes charged in the indictment. The evidence establishes the criminal responsibility of General Lukic on the basis of planning or ordering under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Furthermore, this evidence combined with his failure to discipline units who committed crimes established his criminal responsibility on the basis of instigating, and aiding and abetting by encouraging. Despite his knowledge of the crimes committed by MUP units during this period, that is, the period relevant to the indictment, General Lukic failed to take substantive measures to prevent his subordinates from committing further crimes. And in doing so or failing to do so, he created an atmosphere of impunity, which encouraged and instigated the crimes charged in the indictment. He also aided and abetted the commission of the crimes by permitting, directing, and facilitating the involvement of MUP personnel and resources in the perpetration of these crimes. He knew that without the involvement of the MUP units in Kosovo, the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise could not be achieved, and his role was to employ and engage these units for that or those purposes. By implementing instructions received from the MUP minister in Belgrade and from the Joint Command, he lent material and moral support to the members of the joint criminal enterprise. And by abstaining from taking substantive disciplinary measures against MUP members who committed crimes in Kosovo, he encouraged and morally supported the direct perpetrators of crimes against Kosovo Albanian population. In respect to responsibility under Article 7(3), General Lukic as a commander, as the appointed commander of the MUP staff in Kosovo or for Kosovo and Metohija exercised de jure command over the MUP units, including the special units. I think I already referred the Court to the documents establishing the staff and the jurisdiction of the staff. As a member of the Joint Command, General Lukic also exercised de facto authority over other forces operating under the authority of the Joint Command. He had the material ability, therefore, to prevent crimes from being committed as well as to enforce discipline among MUP units, including special units. As head of the MUP staff, General Lukic had the material ability to issue orders to subordinate officers, including commanders of special units giving such instructions. During the relevant period to the indictment, a functioning discipline and justice system existed to ensure discipline and respect for law within the MUP. The law on internal affairs established a framework for discipline and responsibility and accountability within the MUP, and that is P1016. The decree on discipline and responsibility regulated the duties of MUP superiors to investigate and conduct preliminary proceedings against subordinates who had breached the law. That is P1016, and the Law on Internal Affairs which I cited just now is P1757 [sic]. In addition on the 24th of March, 1999, a decree on internal affairs during the state of war was issued amending the disciplinary responsibilities for MUP officials to some extent in order to take into account the state of war. And this is P993. This decree also indicates that the disciplinary system also existed during the state of war in 1999. This latter decree strengthened the authority of MUP officials to detain suspects, restrict their movement, and perform searches of persons and property. And it made provisions in respect to offences including exhibiting national, racial, or religious intolerance under Article 9 and it simplified the disciplinary system by authorising the head of a sector of the MUP or a person designated by him to discipline without resort to the usual procedures. So there was a structure in place, at least ostensibly, for the prevention and punishment of the persecutory crimes committed against the Kosovar Albanians. As indicated before, General Lukic was informed about these crimes and certainly would have known or would have been put on inquiry notice. The issue as to prevention and punishment of crimes was discussed regularly at MUP staff meetings or MUP meetings with internationals, including the KVM, and I could refer the Court to P2544. Notwithstanding this knowledge, this power and authority that he had, he failed to undertake any or any adequate measures to prevent and punish offenders. Ljubinko Cvetic said that during his tenure in Kosovo - and that is from January 1997 to the end of April 1999 or to April 1999 - he did not know of any cases where police officers were prosecuted for serious crimes against ethnic Albanian people. And that is crimes like murder of Kosovar Albanians, arson of Kosovar Albanian property, or forcible expulsion of Kosovar Albanians from their homes. This Court is entitled to infer that a chief of one of the seven SUPs in Kosovo would be aware if police officers had been so charged or had been so investigated. He never heard of any such investigations or prosecutions at the MUP staff meetings, and this is at pages 8112 to 8113 of the transcript. On the basis of information on relevant investigations and prosecutions requested from the MUP, an OSCE report on the prosecution of war crimes came to the conclusion that the MUP has largely investigated crimes committed by KLA soldiers and only a few cases where potential perpetrators were Serb -- Serbian police or security forces. According to the OSCE, these few investigations conducted against Serbian police or security forces were initiated only when and because the public learnt about the crimes and the MUP had no choice but to conduct investigations. That's P846. This is a general observation made by the OSCE as a result of information it received on request from the MUP. But this Court has before it evidence of a particular situation from a former protected witness who was involved in investigations of the refrigerator truck in which there were bodies found. And it is clear from his evidence in respect to the sequence or the development of that investigation that when the bodies were originally found in the refrigerator truck by the MUP in Kladovo, Serbia, in early April 1999, there was a huge cover-up by the police and that cover-up cloaked the fact that these Albanian civilians or the bodies of these Albanian civilians were found in the river for almost a year until it became public when an intrepid newspaper reporter brought it to the public attention and thereafter the responsibility to investigate became irresistible. That is an example of what the OSCE is discussing about the MUP's attitude in respect to investigations. I don't know if this is a convenient time.

utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honours, there are a couple matters which since we are resuming from break I may raise. utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So we don't have to do this again, it's P2798, Your Honour, not P298.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I had submitted earlier in respect to the Legija group that General Vasiljevic in his statement P2594, paragraph 30, refers to Legija's unit and that is Milorad Ulemek, Legija, his unit involved in the commission of crimes in 1998 -- 1999, I beg your pardon. Paragraph 30 refers to the commission of crimes in Kosovo as indicated by learned counsel by another group known as Legija. However, paragraphs 31, 32, 33 discusses criminal activity and indiscipline by the JSO group under the control of Milorad Ulemek, otherwise known as Legija. So the reference to General Vasiljevic's statement for indiscipline and criminal conduct of this group, this JSO group, is paragraphs 31, 32, and 33 of his statement. The Defence counsel for Mr. Lukic made several submissions in respect to the Prosecution's evidence. He submitted in respect to the 7(3) responsibility, or the responsibility of General Lukic under Article 7(3), that there is no evidence that Lukic had effective control over the MUP units. Counsel says that the plain language meaning and reading of the laws introduced into evidence does not support the claim of superiority authority as to Sreten Lukic and in fact, neither does the other evidence adduced. It is submitted in response, Your Honours, that as head - and the evidence on that I have already outlined - as head of the MUP staff, Lukic -- General Lukic exercised de jure and de facto command over the MUP units including special units. He had the authority to control and coordinate all MUP actions and operations in municipalities throughout Kosovo. I have already referred to the documents appointing him and the documents setting out his area of responsibility. Exhibit P1251 specifically provides that the MUP -- the mandate of the MUP staff was to plan, organise guide, and coordinate the work of the ministry's organisational unit, and the work of units posted or attached to it during their engagement on in the suppression of terrorism in the territory of Kosovo. So even those units that were seconded to Kosovo were within the mandate of the MUP staff. And even in his interview, General Lukic himself said in P948 at pages 37 and 38, that the primary role of the MUP staff was to coordinate, plan, and direct the organisation of the MUP units deployed in Kosovo. So he accepted responsibility, or accepted that the MUP staff that he commanded had responsibility to command and control these units. And I've already referred to P1505 which again sets out the task of the MUP staff. Specific reference can be made and ought to be made, I submit, to the evidence of Ljubinko Cvetic in this area. He said at 8075 of the transcript in respect to the various units, the SAJ, the OPG, the PJP, the JSO, who were sometimes sent from elsewhere in Serbia to come and engage and manoeuvre in Kosovo and Metohija, he accepted that they would be given directives by the MUP staff. He said: "Orders would be submitted to the unit via the MUP staff in Pristina and the direct command of the units was by the commander of the unit in question."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you don't need to go over things that you've been over already with us today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I will move very quickly through these submissions. The other submission was that the OPGs and the PJPs were attached to the secretariats of the interior and commanded by the secretariat of the interior chiefs, not by the MUP staff. Exhibits P1247 and P1249 were cited in support of that submission. These documents are merely lists of persons who are due payment of daily allowances and they show that the SUPs did retain some amount of administrative management of these units; however, again, the evidence of Cvetic was that the secretariats themselves, for manoeuvres and operations, were directly under the MUP headquarters or staff in Pristina. And the expanded MUP staff in Pristina also included the seven SUPs, and that is also demonstrated by P1505. The Defence also submitted that P1505 doesn't support the claim that General Lukic had command over the RDB and that many witnesses, including Cvetic, Byrnes, General DZ, Colonel Ciaglinski, Maisonneuve, Colonel Phillips, et cetera testified that Gajic of the DB was not General Lukic's assistant, but it was rather Colonel Mijatovic. It is submitted that Exhibit 1505 establishes that the MUP staff was established in June 1998 bringing the RDB and the RJB under their control and coordination, or under the control and coordination of the MUP staff headquarters in Pristina. So I respectfully would ask the Court to review Exhibit P1505 in this regard. It clearly states that the expanded MUP staff shall also include the chiefs of the secretariats for internal affairs and branches of the RDB for the zone of Kosovo and Metohija. And this was an order signed, as I indicated before, by the MUP Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. The Defence submission that as head of the MUP staff, General Lukic had no role or authority to discipline MUP members or MUP employees, it is respectfully submitted is not sustainable. There is evidence that he had this power and authority, not only from the decrees that I already referred to dealing with the structures that were in place, but at transcript 8156 in response to a question from the Presiding Judge Bonomy, Mr. Cvetic stated that General Lukic could take disciplinary action against MUP members who committed serious crimes. And this -- this is evidence but this is also a common-sense proposition and inference that the Court could draw from the evidence that the chief of the MUP staff, the police staff, even if he might not be able to get involved in internal infractions of police officers, like uniforms or going to work late or whatever, certainly must have disciplinary influence and impact when offences like murder or arson, et cetera, of the police are being considered. And at that page I just referred to 8156, the transcript reflects that Judge Bonomy asked: "It may be that my question was not properly translated to you. The question was: Assuming the chief of the MUP staff in Pristina, that's Mr. Lukic, were to learn of conduct by MUP officers which amounted to murder, what action would you expect him to take in relation to these offences?" And the witness answered: "He is to notify immediately the head of his organisational unit, that is the chief of the SUP, from where the policeman comes. He is to notify the chief of the public security department." So -- and it follows from his answer when we look at the other evidence that these persons he is to notify also reported to him; he controlled them, that he was more than or he had more than adequate powers to impose discipline for serious crimes on MUP staff. The Defence also submitted that there is no evidence that General Lukic had knowledge of the crimes committed by his subordinates in Kosovo. I have submitted that there were specific complaints made to him and also the circumstances were such that it is inconceivable that the chief of police, the chief of these operations in this area, would not have known about these allegations that were known worldwide. The other submission was that Lukic had no control over the functioning of the judiciary, and therefore could not discipline or punish his superiors. It is submitted that it is not a matter of control over the judiciary; it is a matter of him taking effective steps to ensure that there are appropriate investigations that persons alleged to have committed serious offences are removed from situations where they may commit such offences. And he could take these steps and he had, as I already indicated - and I won't go through all of these decrees - he already had the mechanism, the structure in place to take effective steps if it was his intention to do so. I'll just add that P1736 is the FRY Criminal Code and that code provides that the regular criminal law system, the criminal justice system, also applied to members of the MUP if they committed crimes. The Defence for Mr. -- General Lukic also submitted that the Joint Command is a body with no real power over the MUP. That is contrary to the evidence of General Vasiljevic, General [sic] Cvetic, and even, as I indicated earlier what General Lukic indicated in his interview or inference that can be drawn from what he said in his interview at pages 35 and 36. I've already commented on the incorporation of the Skorpions, a large group, into the MUP and submitted that their deployment and redeployment after having committed such grave crimes as occurred at Podujevo could not have occurred without General Lukic's knowledge. It is respectfully submitted that the several submissions made in respect to the evidence related to General Lukic are unsupported and that, as I've indicated, the Prosecution has presented evidence on which a reasonable Trial Chamber properly directed could act in respect to all the heads of liability and all of the counts charged. With your leave, Your Honours, I'd like to move on to make some general comments about Article 7(3). In respect to all of the accused, we have sought to refer the Court to at least some of the evidence that establishes the several elements of Article 7(3) as it relates to each individual accused. As Mr. Hannis mentioned, three Trial Chambers have now adopted as the practice of the Tribunal the interpretation of Rule 98 bis as amended in 2004, whereby the Trial Chamber need only to find that sufficient evidence to sustain each count of the indictment and need not consider every mode of liability alleged for each count. That is Martic, Mrksic cases, and we said on the 3rd of May, it would apply in the last case in which a no-case submission -- in which Rule 98 bis submission was dealt with, that's the case of Dragomir Milosevic and it seems that the Defence in this case has also accepted that that is the appropriate law and the appropriate practice. So in light of this, the submissions that I make in respect to the general responsibility or that the accused -- each accused is responsible under Article 7(3) of the Statute are necessary -- these submissions are necessary only to extent that the Trial Chamber were, at this stage, to disagree with the Prosecution that there is evidence that the Trial Chamber could rely on under Article 7(1). Article -- or the law in respect to Article 7(3) has been set out in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at -- or from paragraphs 367 forward and I will not address very much in respect to the law. Article 7(3) does not provide a superior with two alternative options when the superior is engaged in discharging his obligations according to international humanitarian law, but it contains two distinct legal obligations: One, to prevent the commission of the offence; and two, to punish the perpetrators. The duty to prevent arises from a superior from the moment he acquires knowledge of or has reason to know that a crime is being or about to be committed. He's not entitled to wait and punish afterwards. And that is from the Strugar trial judgement at page 37 -- at paragraph 373. In this case, the Trial Chamber is entitled to find -- the evidence before the Trial Chamber entitles it to find that, having regard to the history of the crimes against the Kosovar Albanians in the period leading up to the NATO bombing, the first and primary responsibility of each accused was to prevent the crimes. Strict action could have been and ought to have been taken to prevent what happened after the 23rd and the 24th of March, 1999, if there was no intention, shared intention, this these crimes or these events should happen. The accused patently failed to take these measures to put in place specific and stringent measures, if necessary, to prevent the massacres that they said -- or some of them said would occur. And this was despite the fact that each of them, as we have, it is submitted, already demonstrated knew of the pervasive and widespread crimes being committed in 1998. Both military and civilian leaders may be held criminally liable for the acts of their subordinates. The doctrine of command responsibility is ultimately predicated upon the power of a superior to control the acts of his subordinates, and what is required is effective control in the sense of a material ability to prevent or punish criminal conduct. The crucial question is not the civilian -- excuse me, status of the accused but the degree of authority he could exercise over his subordinates. Thus, the concept of effective control for civilian superiors is different to some degree, in that a civilian superior's sanctioning power must be interpreted very broadly and I'm referring now to the Brdjanin trial judgement at paragraph 276, where the observation was made that in respect to the civilian superior sanctioning powers there must be a broad interpretation. It was further said that it cannot be expected that civilian superiors will have disciplinary power over their subordinates equivalent to that of military superiors in an analogous command position. For a finding that civilian superiors have effective control over their subordinates, it suffices that civilian superiors through their position in the hierarchy have the duty to report whenever crimes are committed and that in light of their position the likelihood that those reports will trigger an investigation or initiate a disciplinary or criminal measures is extant. The Court again recognises a situation where the law accords with common sense there, probably with respect to many civilian superiors, will not be a stream-lined situation for the exercise of disciplinary control; however, many times the influence and authority of civilian superiors extends to being able to initiate reports, to raise an alarm. And the higher that civilian superior is, it is -- the alarm that can be raised is raised in higher places can be raised in the very seat of government. And if in raising that alarm and initiating the report and investigation and following up on it, it is possible or there is a likelihood that investigations and disciplinary criminal measures could result, then that has to be considered in respect to civilian superiors. So the material ability -- and I should indicate that that position was also the position in the Aleksovski trial judgement at paragraph 78. The material ability may be the ability to issue orders requiring the competent authorities to take action. It might be able to personally take disciplinary action if the superior has not the power to sanction, it might be just being able to submit reports to competent authorities to take appropriate measures, or to initiate or implement effective investigations or to establish facts and to take active steps to secure that perpetrators will be brought to justice. A superior may only be held criminally responsible for taking such measures that are within his powers, that is within his material possibility, because we are not suggesting that a superior should be obliged to perform the impossible. Effective control is more a matter of evidence than of law. Any evaluation of the action taken by a superior to determine whether his duty has been met is inextricably linked to the facts of each particular situation. What constitutes necessary and reasonable measures required of a commander is a matter not of evidence, but of law. Thus, the categories of material ability are not closed and ought to remain open to the reasonable adjudication of a trial chamber, as command responsibility is the most effective method by which international criminal law can enforce elementary humanitarian values. Much of the analysis not only depends on what could be done but the nature and seriousness of the alleged crimes. Thus, to give an example, in the ICTR case of Musema, M-u-s-e-m-a, where mass murder, genocide, was being considered, it was held that the director of a tea factory had de facto authority over the tea factory employees who were engaged in acts of genocide and used the resources and the -- well, the resources including the facilities, resources, facilities, in the commission of these crimes. The seriousness of a crime imposes on persons who control subordinates in a greater duty to do whatever is possible. In that case, it was held in the judgement at paragraph 880 that a Trial Chamber finds: "The Trial Chamber finds that it had been established beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Musema exercised de jure authority over employees of the Gisovu tea factory while they were on tea factory premises and while they were engaged in their professional duties as employees of the tea factory, even if those duties were performed outside the factory premises. "The Chamber notes that Musema exercised legal and financial control over these employees particularly through his power to appoint and remove these employees from their position at tea factory. The Chamber notes that Musema was in a position by virtue of these powers to take reasonable measures such as removing or threatening to remove an individual from his or her position in the tea factory if he or she was identified as a perpetrator of crimes punishable under the Statute." I give the example of the civilian in this situation to emphasise that this category, it is something that should be left to the assessment of a Trial Chamber, having heard all the evidence. The formal designation as a commander or a superior not a necessary prerequisite for superior responsibility. This consideration as to whether or not somebody is formally designated a commander or superior is particularly in the case concerning Mr. Sainovic. We know that he was head of the group responsible for contact with the -- with the various international bodies that operated in Kosovo and that he was a deputy minister -- one of five deputy ministers of the FRY. He was not formally designated commander of the MUP forces in Kosovo or the defence, local defence forces, in Kosovo or the VJ in Kosovo. However, the evidence of his conduct mainly but not exclusively, from Generals -- from General Vasiljevic and Mr. Cvetic taken at its highest is that he exercised de facto control and authority over the commands of the forces of the FRY in Kosovo at the material time. I refer back in particular to the citation or the extensive quotation I made from the evidence of General Vasiljevic at the beginning of my address in respect to Mr. Sainovic. The Joint Command was a commanding body as well as a coordinating organ and the evidence, it is submitted, makes it clear that Mr. Sainovic effectively headed that body. Superior/subordinate relationship based on a notion of control within a hierarchy, or is based on the notion of control within a hierarchy, but control can be exercised in a direct or indirect manner. There is no requirement that the perpetrator must be in a direct chain of command under the superior. I refer to the Celebici appeals judgement at paragraph 251. Direct and indirect relationships within the hierarchy is possible. Again, the Brdjanin trial judgement at page 276 accepted this. Thus, Mr. Milutinovic -- or if Mr. Milutinovic or Mr. Sainovic in their formal or de facto positions could make reports or initiate investigations that could -- that had a likelihood of resulting in the restraint or punishment of the direct perpetrators, they can be held liable if they fail to do so, even if these direct perpetrators were not in a direct chain of command below either of them. But in any case, in addition to this, both Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic exercised effective control over the military and police generals that were involved in actively furthering the JCE on the ground. Having regard to this or the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted, Your Honours, that prior to the period or prior to the 24th of March, 1999, in accordance with his duty to prevent and after that day in accordance with his duty to punish, the accused Mr. Milutinovic could have exercised his substantial authority and influence as president of Serbia to order the MUP and its senior members to report to him within 48 hours on the allegations of abuses of Kosovar Albanian citizens by forces of the FRY, to report to him on their investigations and prosecutions of the perpetrators, and to report to him on any other appropriate measures to be adopted. It is submitted that he also could have used his legal authority as a member of the Supreme Defence Council to convene Supreme Defence Council meetings to place on agenda issues re allegations of crimes committed by the VJ, to put in place systems to bring offenders to justice. In failing to do, or to do adequately in the circumstances any of these things he is liable under Article 7(3) of the Rules. Indeed, Your Honours, he had power and significant influence over the careers of some of the alleged senior perpetrators, both MUP and the VJ; instead, as has been seen, he appointed and promoted them. It is submitted that Mr. Sainovic as de facto head of the Joint Command had the responsibility as commanders of the VJ and MUP to take effective steps to prevent or punish crimes including ordering investigations and referring cases to military or civilian courts. Mr. Sainovic was in a position to report effectively to the competent authorities. We have seen that he was occasionally sent on fact-finding missions to gain insight into the events in Kosovo. He was able to submit reports to the SDC and other competent authorities about allegations of crimes in Kosovo and he was able to make recommendations as to their prevention and the punishment of the perpetrators. In failing to exercise these powers to prevent or punish the crimes, he's also liable under 7(3). Indeed, I refer back to P1000, that is the minutes of, I think, the 5th Session of the SDC, in any case, the minutes of an SDC meeting in the latter part of 1998, in which Mr. Milutinovic was present when Mr. Sainovic reported to the SDC on cooperation between the VJ and MUP among other security-related issues concerning Kosovo. Both of them, it is clear from these exhibits, were in a position to express persuasive opinions, at least, in the SDC either as informant or decision-maker. And in addition, we have the evidence of Mr. Cvetic already discussed in respect to the several MUP meetings that Mr. Sainovic attended in which he was able to give instructions to the leaders of the MUP. I'll touch on briefly, if I may, some of the items of evidence that also establishes -- where it may well be said establishes intent to commit these crimes but certainly establishes a failure to take appropriate steps to prevent and punish these crimes. There is evidence that the -- that VJ and MUP subordinates were sent to Kosovo without proper training and education in the lawful behaviour in armed conflicts. Volunteers were accepted without screening and units known for their criminal propensity were sent to Kosovo. Again I refer the Chamber to the evidence of Goran Stoparic. He is someone who indicated that after the crime in Podujevo he was expecting punishment, people to be fined or demoted, but that didn't happen. Vasiljevic's testimony in his statement P2594 about Arkan's Tigers being part of Radosavljevic's unit committing crimes in Kosovo discussed in a meeting with Mr. Sainovic present. The evidence of insiders, VJ insiders, K54, K82, K89, who said that they were sent into action in Kosovo with only a couple months' training and no instructions on the law of war and responsibility to civilians. Evidence of K79, a PJP member - that's a policeman like Goran Stoparic - who also was not given any instructions, when sent to Kosovo, on appropriate behaviour. In respect to the VJ and the MUP, the evidence is that very few, if any, serious investigations were done on crimes, serious crimes, committed against Kosovar Albanians. In assessing this, the Tribunal would, no doubt, have a look at the evidence as to the widespread and gross nature of these crimes. I've already referred to the report by the OSCE indicating that even after the conflict there was a hesitancy to investigate the crimes and investigations were only done when something became too public to ignore. Exhibits P829 and 830 are -- P829 is a letter from the VJ to the OSCE on investigations and prosecutions done, and it demonstrates basically the same, little or nothing done. Exhibit P831 similarly is a letter of the MUP to the OSCE, it demonstrates the same thing. There were investigations, there was some work done, but in respect to the investigations of these serious and gross offences against Kosovar Albanians, very little. Similarly P845. Lakic Djorovic testified before this Tribunal; his statement is P2671. He said that many state security organs and military prosecutors even resided in the apartments of expelled Kosovar Albanians. And some VJ representatives who stole cars of Kosovar Albanians. P953 was a document that was tendered in the Milosevic case, and it is a report on the work of military judicial organs during the state of war from 21st -- up to the 21st of June, 1999, and it shows that 88 per cent of cases were related to acts committed against the VJ by its members; only 12 per cent were related to what were described as other crimes. Similarly P954, a similar report. An analysis of this report and the previous one shows there are various serious crimes against Kosovar Albanians are investigated. They cover mainly property crimes and disciplinary crimes against VJ members.
