utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may need double-checking, but our records show that P953 and P954 are not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that my friend is right. What I'm trying to find out is whether or not there is an outstanding application in respect to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Neither is admitted according to our records, Mr. Stamp, and as far as we are concerned all applications for the admission of evidence have been disposed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I withdraw any reference to those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to Lakic Djorovic, when crimes became known, security organs of the VJ sometimes undertook steps to dispose of the crimes before they could be prosecuted. Military prosecutors who wanted to prosecute army members were sabotaged and threatened. And this is in his statement P2671 at paragraphs 45, paragraph 6, paragraph 29, paragraph 31 and 38. Even after the war, he himself was continually threatened and put under pressure because he tried to prosecute, as a military prosecutor, crimes that he became aware of in Kosovo, P2671, paragraphs 1, 4, and 57. Similarly, the MUP investigated very few MUP members for the serious crimes. I have already referred to the documents. Ljubinko Cvetic, the -- was head of a SUP, as I indicated, said that as head of the SUP he did not know of any serious -- of any police officer, certainly no serious [sic] police officer being charged for any serious offence against Kosovar Albanians. Your Honours had the evidence about Mr. Stevanovic's notebook and the meeting with the MUP and Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Sainovic in which it is indicated that Mr. Milosevic spoke about mopping up the terrain being the most important and that traces along roads are to be removed, no corpse, no crime. The indicators, especially the 828 bodies in Serbia, and the circumstances after such long delay in which these investigations started indicate that instead of investigating, the prevailing intention was to cover up. In respect to knowledge required under Article 7(3), the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief covers the law in respect to knowledge. There -- the requirement is either actual knowledge or constructive knowledge or that the accused knew of the offences or ought -- or had reason to know that the act was about to be committed or had been committed. I certainly will not trouble the Court with the law in respect to knowledge. But I may, with respect, refer the Court to the indicia given by the United Nations Commission of Experts in its final report on armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, which was referred to in the Celebici trial judgement at paragraph 386. In that judgement the Court said that in determining whether a superior in fact must have possessed the required knowledge, the Trial Chamber may consider the indicia stated by the commission of experts. So the -- a Trial Chamber may impute actual knowledge from circumstantial evidence and the indicia that the commission of experts said -- used in their report, affirmed in Celebici, included the number of illegal acts, the type of illegal acts, the scope of illegal acts, the time during which the illegal acts occurred, the number and type of troops involved, the logistics involved, the geographic location of the acts, the widespread occurrence of the acts, the tactical tempo of operations, modus operandi of similar illegal acts, the officers and the staff involved. It is respectfully submitted that applying or considering these matters, this Court is entitled to infer that each accused must have had actual knowledge about the crimes alleged in the indictment. In the alternative, each of the accused was possessed of sufficiently alarming information, to use the expression adopted in the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber in paragraph 154, which put him on notice of possible unlawful acts by subordinates and therefore each accused had reason to know that these crimes would be committed or had been committed. Exhibits -- Your Honours, I should have cited Exhibits 1912 to 19 -- sorry, 1912 -- P1912, P1939, P1940, P1941, which are reports from the 3rd Army command organ for legal affairs on the work of the military prosecutions office between the 12th of April and the 30th of May. These documents also show that investigations and prosecutions were limited to minor offences, particularly violations of military discipline. I postpone referring to them to check if they were in fact in evidence. And while I'm on this point, Your Honours, Exhibits 953 and 954, which I referred to and which my friend Mr. O'Sullivan indicated that the records show that they were not in evidence. I agree that the record shows they were not in evidence, but I think that there may have been an error in the official evidence register. At page 11509 of the transcript of the 12th of March, 2007, the -- this exchange took place at the end of the evidence of Mr. Djorovic, or during the evidence of Mr. Djorovic. Question by Presiding Judge Bonomy: "Now, in your statement in paragraph 62 and the following you referred to a number of exhibits or a number of documents that were shown to you when you gave the statement, documents that were received in another case in the Tribunal through a Defence witness for Mr. Milosevic." To which my learned colleague, Ms. Moulin, applied: "Your Honours, I do not intend to go with the witness through these documents because I think he has in his written statement commented on them. I would just like to give you the cross-reference to the exhibit number: The document in paragraph 52 of the statement is Exhibit 593; the document referred to in paragraph 53 of his statement is P2826; the document referred to in paragraph 54 of his statement is Exhibit P2825; and the document referred to in paragraph 55 and 56 is Exhibit P954. President Bonomy said: "Thank you." I believe from that that if the documents were not officially entered into the evidence register, it is due to error, and I would apply now that that matter be reviewed. And if the documents properly ought to be in evidence that they be so received and that the Tribunal is therefore entitled to rely upon them. Before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you say, Mr. Stamp, does indicate that these have, in fact, been admitted and the record of exhibits admitted erroneously excludes them. If that causes any prejudice to the Defence, we'll hear any further submissions they have to make about the impact of these documents, but following the practice that we have consistently applied throughout the trial they were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I close, there are some matters which I wish to make the Prosecution's position clear about. During submissions on the interviews of each accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise interfering. Mr. Stamp, I just would request you to help me understand a proposition -- a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You see, invariably in the constitutions of the world there is a clause given which is an article given which speaks of the rules which are to be made under the constitution. As a subordinate legislation, for purposes of running the government and for running departments inter-se and that is followed by other subordinate departments as well. So they lay down what will be the relationship between one department and its subordinates and the other and so on and so forth. Now, I was wondering if you have knowledge of any such rules of business as these are usually called in respect of this country we are dealing with; and if you have, can you kindly supply us with a copy because that would give a more clearer picture of how one has to behave and how one has to conduct relationship as these emerge inter-se the various departments, the groups, the branches, and so on. But if you come to the conclusion that there is none, please also let us know. That will be quite an unusual thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan has raised a matter which requires debate by the Bench, so we will have to adjourn to deal with that. We're approaching the break in any event, and we will resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're grateful to the Defence, I think Mr. Zecevic in particular, who has provided reference to some material which deals with the point raised by Judge Chowhan and we of course have had regard to other documents already in the process which supplement that and deal with the matter. So we are now satisfied that that has been dealt with, Mr. Stamp, and we can hear the balance of your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to just cover a few miscellaneous matters before I close, Your Honours. An issue arose as to what use the Court ought to make of the statements made by each accused in respect to the other accused. At page -- at paragraph 22 of the Prosecution's filing on the 18th of August, 2006, in which we responded -- or replied to the Defence response to application to tender the statements of the accused, the Prosecution set out its position and we wish to make it clear that we do not resile from it or seek to renege upon this. And at paragraph 22 we state that: "The Prosecution clarifies its motion to indicate that the statements are to be used in their entirety as evidence against the proponent of the statement and against the co-accused except portions that address the acts and conduct of mental state of other accused." The second matter relates to a statement I made on Friday in respect to the evidence of Ambassador Petritsch in which I stated that the ambassador could not recall whether there were two statements made by two persons about a massacre of Albanians or whether there was one statement made by either Mr. Milutinovic or Mr. Stambuk. That is not correct. The ambassador did state on more than one occasion that there were two statements. He did so in his direct examination at transcript 10637 in which an answer to the President of the Chamber, Judge Bonomy. "Q. Well, are these -- do you think these are two separate occasions? "A. That was -- there were, to my recollection, two separate occasions." And further on in cross-examination at 10841 he said: "Clearly at the time when I was interviewed by the ICTY obviously this one example came to my mind and not Mr. Milutinovic's example. Once I re-read the dispatch I was reminded that the same had happened also in a conversation with Mr. Milutinovic." And he also said it again at 1078 -- or, sorry, at 10879. I had referred the Court to the decision in the Simic case, the events which -- they were the events at Bosanski Samac. I should note that the Appeals Chamber in that case dismissed the conviction of Simic under the joint criminal enterprise; however, this -- right, dismissed the conviction or set aside the conviction, I should say, of Simic on the joint criminal enterprise. This decision, to set aside the conviction, was based on the technical ground that there was insufficient notice in the indictment in respect to the joint criminal enterprise. So that decision does not derogate from the Appeals Court finding that the Trial Chamber was entitled to make the inferences about Simic's intent that I submitted upon and which was the basis for his conviction on other grounds. And finally in respect to Mr. Milutinovic, I have been reminded to add, in respect to de facto authority - and this is in respect to both Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic - that they were both members of the Main Board of the SPS, the Socialist Party of Serbia, and that can be seen in P1012, P1012, and they were both present at the meeting of the 10th of June, 1998, when a coordination body to deal with the situation in Kosovo was set up by Mr. Milutinovic -- Mr. Milosevic. Milomir Minic was to become head of that body and Dusan Matkovic and Zoran Andjelkovic members, and that is from pages 79 forward of that same exhibit I just referred to. This body later evolved to become the Joint Command, and as my colleague Mr. Hannis indicated in respect to P1317 which is an RFA response from the Serbian authorities, the Joint Command was created without a legal basis. From this it is submitted that the members of the Joint Command, including Mr. Milutinovic -- sorry, the members of the joint criminal enterprise, including Mr. Milutinovic, used a system of parallel information and decision-making chains, the SPS in this case, to further their criminal aims. And Exhibit P2828 is an example of this. This is a letter sent by Vojislav Zivkovic to Mr. Milutinovic. The letter was not just expressing concern of -- of a local low-level Serb politician, as suggested by Mr. O'Sullivan, but it also asked for Serbs to be armed, for local Serbs to be armed and to be organised into formations. Exhibit P0 -- sorry, P1012 shows that Mr. Zivkovic was also a member of the SPS Main Board. So this is a situation of the Joint Command being created informally and persons, local politicians, Zivkovic, who was president of the SPS Kosovo Provincial Board could also make informal requests to the leadership, which as the evidence indicates were eventually carried out. Those, may it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, are the submissions on behalf of the Prosecution in answer to the submission made by learned counsel for the Defence under Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the only specific decision of the SPS that you rely on? I mean in the case as a whole, have you made earlier submissions about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, that is the one we rely on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Hannis, I wish to thank the Court for the opportunity to respond to the submissions made by learned counsel on the other side. May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, you indicated you may wish to make submission about the use to which the statement of one accused may be made in the case against another accused. Do you have anything further to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if I've understood my friend correctly he seems to be withdrawing that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's taking a position that was set out in the response -- the reply to your response seeking -- when the Prosecution sought to have these documents admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. We had lodged our objection there. One final point which may be another point for verification. In Friday's transcript, I'm referring to page 12695, line 22, submissions were made in respect to Exhibit P508, and our records again show that P508 is not admitted into evidence. Those are submissions made in respect to Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I gather that was used in the course of evidence on the 4th of April, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 4th of April -- 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, last Friday, that's when the submissions were made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The document to which you're referring was part of the evidence on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it wasn't. It's not in the transcript, it's never been tendered. There's no reference to P508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing everyone can rest assured about is that every exhibit to which reference has been made in these submissions will be checked by the Trial Chamber before the decision on these motions is issued. If, however - and it's perhaps inevitable in view of the volume of material here - if something comes to light indicating the possibility that either an exhibit which was not, in fact, admitted may mistakenly be referred to or the opposite, that one properly admitted might be overlooked, then parties should, by e-mail, address that issue on notice to the other side by directing the attention of the Trial Chamber to that possibility. Now, in light of these comments, are there any other matters that Defence counsel wish to raise? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to finish up on the matter that I had raised during Mr. Stamp's submissions, there was a portion of the Vasiljevic statement that was referred to and then the conclusions therefrom were referred to multiple times today by Mr. Stamp beginning at transcript page 2, lines 7 through 14 today, dealing with the former Skorpion members who were part of the reserve SAJ elements, stating that they had committed additional crimes after being redeployed in Gnjilane. I would like to point out on January 23rd and 24th, General Vasiljevic negated that portion of his statement first at page 9004, line 23, all the way through transcript page 9005, line 12, wherein he stated he knew of no crimes committed by the SAJ reserve elements upon their deployment after Podujevo. And then in re-direct from questioning by Mr. Hannis who specifically asked about the Gnjilane incident at transcript page 9107, lines 1 through 17, stating that this was not an incident tied to either the SAJ and the Skorpions or any MUP unit. And then that's basically the thrust of the one correction I had. There were two other matters that I think will be self-evident namely that the Goran Stoparic exhibit P2224 is actually devoid to any reference to Lukic or the MUP staff. So Mr. Stamp's submission on that regard were incorrect. And then also the Vasiljevic statement at paragraph 31, 32, and 33 referenced at transcript page 28, lines 16 through 18, although those paragraphs do identify the JSO and delineate the chain of command of the JSO, there is again no reference to Lukic or the staff. And importantly there is no reference to any crimes, as was represented by Mr. Stamp in his submissions. Those are just -- the first is the most important one because I don't think that would necessarily have been caught since the statement says one thing but the witness when he came here modified that somewhat. So I wanted to bring that to Your Honours' attention so it's easier to locate these things when you are preparing your decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course that I don't want to enter a polemic with my learned friend Mr. Stamp, I just want to indicate a few situations where, quite simply, what he read out to you is simply not written. On 12704, page 12704, from Friday, speaking of P1468, my colleague Mr. Stamp said that this document shows that Sainovic attended 60 meetings as the person in charge; however, there is no reference to any such thing on a single page of this document. Please look it up. Also 12701, another page reference from Friday. I quote: "P2594 is the Vasiljevic statement, paragraphs 78 to 82," again he is quoting it in the context of this evidence that Sainovic was at the head of the Joint Command. However, in the mentioned paragraphs there is no reference to this. It was stated that he sat at the head of the table but it -- there is no reference to Sainovic being at the head of the Joint Command. Also, Your Honours, today on page 2, line 19 of the transcript, what is analysed is a Prosecution Exhibit 2594, Vasiljevic again. Reference is made to the system of information Sainovic established in relation to the army and the MUP. However, I did not find that anywhere in this document. Also, when speaking of Mr. Lukic and quoting P298 -- 2948, this is page -- line 14 today and he also says that Sainovic was at the head of the Joint Command. Your Honours, if you simply look at these pages of these documents, there is no reference to that, there is no mention of that. Finally, on page 44, line 24, today, when speaking of Stevanovic's notebook and meetings that were allegedly attended by Sainovic, according to that notebook, 8828 is the transcript page reference, Vasiljevic decidedly stated that he was not at that meeting, that he did not know anything about this, everything he said he is saying on the basis of the papers shown to him by the OTP when he came to this Tribunal. Thank you, Your Honours, and I believe this will be of assistance when you make your decision. Thank you. Your Honour, I just want to say page 56, line 21, P948 is the reference here not 2948, as is in the transcript now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would like to give an indication this afternoon of when we will issue our determination on this. We'll need to adjourn to consider that and we'll resume at 20 minutes to, which will simply be for the purpose of intimating the date when the decision will be issued. --- Break taken at 1.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will give its decision on the afternoon of the 18th of May, that's a week on Friday, at 2.15. We're now adjourned until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
